clue.text: Is this a dance or what? (6,2)

blocks.note: a ballroom dance named after the phrase said when tapping a dancer's shoulder to cut in
the polite 'Pardon?' when you have not heard or cannot believe what was said

explanation.surface: Somebody on a crowded floor wondering aloud whether this shuffle counts as dancing.
explanation.walkthrough: The question frame hides that the clue is two senses side by side. An excuse-me dance, where you tap a dancer's shoulder to cut in, is a British ballroom custom.
explanation.definitionFit: An excuse-me is a dance where partners can be claimed by others, and 'Excuse me?' is an incredulous 'What?'.

clue.text: Butcher’s report of Tour de France? (6)

indicators.note: A report is a sound, so what is wanted is how the next phrase sounds when spoken, not its spelling.

blocks.note: the 'tower of France' is the Eiffel Tower

explanation.surface: A butcher reporting on the cycle race round France.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tour de France' wants to be the bike race; read it as French for 'tower' and it is the Eiffel. A butcher's is rhyming slang: butcher's hook = look.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a butcher's is having a look, and getting an eyeful is taking a good look.

clue.text: Caught up with old men for casual drinks (6)

blocks.note: c = caught, the cricket scorecard abbreviation
taken as it stands
pa = father, the old man; two of them

explanation.surface: Catching up with some elderly men over informal drinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Caught up' looks like one phrase but splits into the cricket abbreviation and a plain word. 'Old man' for a father is familiar slang; a cuppa is a British cup of tea.
explanation.definitionFit: A cuppa is an informal cup of tea, so cuppas are casual drinks.

clue.text: Teacher in old college wasting time (3)

indicators.note: To waste something is to lose it, so the word after it is thrown out of the letters.

blocks.note: 'college' is old slang for prison, and stir is prison
t = time, removed

explanation.surface: A teacher at a former college, idling the hours away.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads 'old college' as a university; it is dated slang for prison, which is stir. Sir is what British pupils call a male teacher.
explanation.definitionFit: British schoolchildren address a male teacher as Sir, so the word stands for the teacher.

clue.text: Firing left and right, say (8,6)

blocks.note: dismissal from a job, not the shooting of guns
'Left, right!' is what a drill sergeant calls to troops on the march

explanation.surface: Guns going off on both sides.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface paints a battle with shots on both flanks; 'firing' means sacking, and left and right are the calls of a parade ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Marching orders are a dismissal from a job, and 'left, right' are literally orders given to marching soldiers.

clue.text: Warrior caste member’s clash over 7 (6)

indicators.note: Something turned over is upside down, so the word before it is read backwards.

blocks.note: colours that jar clash
7 down is POSITION; to position something is to put it

explanation.surface: A member of a warrior caste getting into a fight.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference points at the answer of 7 down, taken as a verb. Rajputs are a Hindu warrior caste of northern India.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rajputs are a caste of northern India traditionally associated with soldiering, so one is a warrior caste member.

clue.text: A star drinks litre in mineral water (11)

indicators.note: What something drinks goes inside it, so the star takes the next letters into itself.

blocks.note: taken as it stands
the Pole Star
l = litre
taken as it stands

explanation.surface: A celebrity downing a litre of fizzy water.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Star' wants to be a celebrity; it is the Pole Star. Apollinaris is a German sparkling mineral water brand.
explanation.definitionFit: Apollinaris is a naturally carbonated German mineral water sold by that name.

clue.text: I’m leaving tax office (8)

indicators.note: Whatever is leaving goes away, so those letters come out of the word that follows.

blocks.note: taken as it stands, removed
an imposition is a tax or levy

explanation.surface: Someone announcing their departure from the tax office.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tax office' reads as one institution; it is two parts, the wordplay and the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An office is a post or position held, as in the office of mayor.

clue.text: Singer against “The King of Pop” singles (3,5)

blocks.note: pressed against = pressed to, as in cheek to cheek
Michael Jackson, known as the King of Pop, by his initials
singles = ones

explanation.surface: A singer campaigning against the King of Pop's hit records.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singles' wants to be records beside a pop singer; it is just ones. Tom Jones is the Welsh singer of 'It's Not Unusual'.
explanation.definitionFit: Tom Jones is a Welsh pop singer with a career running from the 1960s.

clue.text: “Head of firm” same in translation? (5,9)

indicators.note: Translating rearranges words into a new form, so the letters of the quoted phrase and 'same' are rearranged.

blocks.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A query: is 'head of firm' the same thing once put into another language?
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: rearrange the letters and you get the French for a businessman, which is roughly what a head of firm is.
explanation.definitionFit: Homme d'affaires is French for businessman, the kind of person who heads a firm, so it is 'Head of firm' translated.

clue.text: Italian city about to welcome a ruler (7)

indicators.note: Turned about means facing the other way, so the city's name is read backwards.
A host welcomes a guest in, so the reversed city takes the next letters inside it.

blocks.note: the Italian capital
'a' as in 'five pounds a head' means per

explanation.surface: Rome preparing to receive a visiting monarch.
explanation.walkthrough: The small word 'a' is the one to watch: it stands for PER, as prices are quoted 'a' or 'per' item.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym by example: an emperor is the highest kind of monarch, one who reigns over an empire.

clue.text: Crossing river is big problem for marsupial (7)

indicators.note: To cross a river is to span it, so the outer letters stretch around the river's name.

blocks.note: OS = outsize, the clothing label
the Po, Italy's longest river
a sum is an arithmetic problem

explanation.surface: An animal facing a big obstacle in getting over a river.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures an animal stuck at a riverbank; 'big problem' is two pieces, the outsize label and a school sum, which together span the river.
explanation.definitionFit: The opossum is an American marsupial that carries its young in a pouch.

clue.text: American country music embraces Democrat protest song (2,3,4)

indicators.note: What embraces something holds it in its arms, so the anthem takes D inside it.

blocks.note: US = American
a country's music is its national anthem
D = Democrat

explanation.surface: An American country track that takes in a Democratic protest number.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Country music' wants to be the Nashville genre; it is a national anthem. 'Us and Them' is a Pink Floyd song from The Dark Side of the Moon about war and division.
explanation.definitionFit: Pink Floyd's 'Us and Them' is an anti-war song, so it can be called a protest song.

clue.text: Part of house contract put in order (7,4)

blocks.note: to draw in is to contract, as days do in autumn
to groom is to make neat

explanation.surface: Part of a house sale agreement being tidied up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Contract' looks like a noun from a house purchase; it is the verb, to shrink.
explanation.definitionFit: A definition by example: the formal reception room, originally the 'withdrawing room' guests retired to, is one room among many in a house.

clue.text: Bathroom walls dry in house (5)

indicators.note: Walls surround a space, so the bathroom word goes round the letters for dry.

blocks.note: loo is British slang for a lavatory
TT = teetotal, not drinking

explanation.surface: A home's bathroom walls drying out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'House' wants to be a building; it is the game, also called housey-housey, whose winning call is 'House!'. It is the old British name for bingo, a close relative of lotto.
explanation.definitionFit: House, or housey-housey, is a numbers game of the lotto or bingo type.

clue.text: Return from work (6,6)

blocks.note: not a homecoming but a yield, what an investment or effort pays back
not leaving the office but the source of that yield: pay for labour, as opposed to interest or dividends

explanation.surface: Coming home at the end of the working day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Return from work' reads as the commute home; the return here is what work pays, the phrase used on a tax return.
explanation.definitionFit: Earned income is money received from employment, the return one's work produces.

clue.text: Set about securing opening for roofs (8)

indicators.note: Turned about means the other way round, so 'set' is reversed.
To secure something is to hold it fast, so the reversed word holds the opening inside.

blocks.note: taken as it stands
a hatch is an opening in a wall or deck

explanation.surface: Someone getting on with fastening an opening in the roofs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Roofs' is a verb here, matching 'thatches', not the plural noun the surface suggests.
explanation.definitionFit: To thatch a house is to roof it with straw or reeds, so thatches means roofs.

clue.text: Supporter upset with corrupt trial of judges (8)

indicators.note: An upset thing is knocked over, so the supporter is read backwards.
Something corrupt is spoilt from its proper form, so the letters of 'trial' are rearranged.

blocks.note: a bra is a supporting garment
anagram fodder

explanation.surface: A backer angry at a rigged trial before the bench.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a courtroom; 'Supporter' is not a backer but the undergarment.
explanation.definitionFit: Arbitral means relating to arbiters or arbitrators, people who judge disputes.

clue.text: Solo player cross after air horn’s blasted (8,4)

indicators.note: What comes after is placed later, so the cross follows the rearranged letters.
Something blasted is blown apart, so the letters of 'air horn's' are scattered and rearranged.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, with the S of the possessive
to ford a river is to cross it

explanation.surface: A lone musician getting cross after an air horn goes off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Solo player' reads as a lone musician, but it is the actor who played Han Solo in Star Wars.
explanation.definitionFit: Harrison Ford played Han Solo in Star Wars, so he is the player of Solo.

clue.text: Heading for meal, I will have place setting (6)

indicators.note: The heading of a word is its first letter.

blocks.note: its first letter
taken as it stands
lieu is French for place, as in 'in lieu of'

explanation.surface: Someone at dinner claiming a particular place setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Place setting' reads as cutlery laid for one diner; the two words split between wordplay and definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A milieu is a person's surroundings or social setting.

clue.text: Old leaves beginning to separate from husks and straw (6)

indicators.note: Whatever leaves goes away, so 'old' drops out of the word that follows.

blocks.note: taken as it stands, removed
the threshold of something is its beginning

explanation.surface: Last year's leaves starting to break away from the husks and straw on a farm.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old leaves' looks like fallen foliage; 'leaves' is a verb, telling OLD to depart.
explanation.definitionFit: To thresh grain is to beat it to separate the seed from the husks and straw.

clue.text: Dilute good cup of tea (5)

blocks.note: to thin a liquid is to dilute it
g = good

explanation.surface: Advice to water down a decent cup of tea.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface is about brewing, but 'cup of tea' is the idiom for something one likes: not my cup of tea, not my thing.
explanation.definitionFit: Something that is your cup of tea is your thing, what suits you.

clue.text: Handles bent as it was held (5,4)

indicators.note: 'Bent as' is the start of 'bent as a nine-bob note', very bent; bent letters are twisted into a new order.

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 9 letters

explanation.surface: Door handles that were bent from the way they were gripped.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Handles' reads as a noun, the thing held; it is the verb. 'Bent as a nine-bob note' is a British phrase for thoroughly crooked, there never having been a nine-shilling note.
explanation.definitionFit: To deal with a problem is to handle it.

clue.text: Bear or horse shelter (7)

blocks.note: horse is slang for heroin, whose abbreviation is H
an arbour is a leafy shelter in a garden

explanation.surface: A choice of animals seeking shelter: a bear or a horse.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface offers a menagerie; 'Bear' is the verb, as in bearing a grudge. H for horse comes by way of heroin.
explanation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of holding a feeling: one can bear or harbour a grudge, a hope or a suspicion alike.

clue.text: Lettuce and eggs sliced by chief (7)

indicators.note: A thing sliced by a knife has the knife go through its middle, so the chief goes inside the eggs.

blocks.note: roe is fish eggs
main = chief, principal

explanation.surface: A salad of lettuce with eggs cut up by the head cook.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Chief' wants to be the head chef in this kitchen scene; it is the adjective, main.
explanation.definitionFit: Romaine is the American and French name for cos lettuce.

clue.text: Not so hot when skirt’s lifted (3)

indicators.note: In a down clue, lifting a word turns it upwards, so it reads from the bottom.

blocks.note: to skirt is to edge, and so is to hem

explanation.surface: Feeling a bit cooler once one's skirt is raised.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not so hot' reads as temperature; it is the slang judgement 'unimpressive', which is what 'meh' says.
explanation.definitionFit: Meh is a shrug of a word meaning mediocre, nothing special: not so hot.

clue.text: Spicy meat used in dishes à la Milanese (6)

indicators.note: What is used in the dishes is inside them, so the answer runs inside the following words.

blocks.note: disheS A LA MIlanese

explanation.surface: Spicy meat that goes into Milan-style cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: The accent on à does not count in the grid. Salami is itself Italian, which suits the Milanese surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Salami is a spiced, cured sausage eaten cold in slices.

clue.text: Like a bad shot — horrible! (2,6)

indicators.note: Something gone bad is out of its proper state, so the letters of 'a shot' are rearranged.

blocks.note: anagram fodder
anagram fodder, with 'a' either side of the indicator
ugh is the exclamation of disgust

explanation.surface: A golfer's verdict on a dreadful stroke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like' reads as a comparison word opening the sentence; as the definition it is the conjunction, as in 'it looks like it will rain'.
explanation.definitionFit: Informally 'like' serves as a conjunction meaning as though: he acted like he owned the place.
